extracted.intended_audience: Parliamentarians, government policymakers, legislators, and officials designing or supervising independent administrative agencies (Canadian context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for structuring political, executive, parliamentary and judicial controls over independent administrative agencies, and for drafting enabling and subordinate legislation and procedures. Focus is on balancing agency independence with accountability, procedural safeguards, and judicial deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary review and use of existing tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should take swift and concrete action to review agencies given independence from the executive and should develop ways to put to good use the tools it already has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Parliament fails to use its tools, complaints that it has lost control will be empty. Implication: legislative committees and existing parliamentary mechanisms should be actively used to hold agencies accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and characteristics of political appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Political appeals are statutory rights to apply to Cabinet or a minister to review an agency decision, producing a correlative executive power to determine the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political appeals differ from court appeals (they raise policy, not fact or law), typically lack procedural requirements, can coexist with lobbying, decisions are rarely supported by reasons, and Cabinet appeals are often highly secretive. Example: s.64(1) National Transportation Act petitions to Governor in Council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks and unsuitability of political appeals for agency decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Political appeals are overly susceptible to extraneous influences and political imperatives and therefore inappropriate where agencies were established to be insulated from mainstream politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversing agency decisions for partisan reasons harms integrity, credibility and morale. Political appeals do not adequately achieve (a) meritorious review for participants or (b) a proper mechanism for political control of agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of adjudicative appeals and political intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: True rights of appeal for participants should be established within an adjudicative framework; Cabinet powers to reverse decisions should be exercised through a vehicle suited to intrusive political powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament should not require Cabinet to set public policy in the context of a specific case or through processes cloaked in adjudicative language such as 'appeal' or 'review'. Avoid 'judicializing' political appeals by imposing judicial procedural safeguards on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive intervention via Cabinet on own initiative (if authorized)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Parliament authorizes executive intervention, it should give Cabinet (rather than a single minister) the power to act on its own initiative and bring the matter clearly into the political arena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: (1) limits availability/use to matters of genuine public importance, (2) divorces the agency from the political decision preserving its independent image. Model preferred to petition-triggered appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of political intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: While there is reason to preclude executive intervention until the agency has rendered its decision (to develop a public record), intervention should be allowed at any point if it is known from the outset that a political solution will likely be imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-decision intervention aids Cabinet accountability and focuses judgment on relevant issues; however, where Cabinet is determined to intervene early, waiting may be futile and unnecessary delay should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of interested persons to make representations in political interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet, having taken decisional authority away from an agency, should allow interested persons an opportunity to make representations before its decision is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The political nature of the decision does not reduce the value of representations or of building a record. One mechanism is to convert agency decision-making into an inquiry and let the agency provide recommendations to inform Cabinet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns about systematic executive approvals of agency decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'executive approval' model (agency decisions subject to executive approval) integrates executive intervention as a normal part of decision-making and risks confusion about agency criteria and influence on agency behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems include agencies tailoring decisions to what they think will meet approval, masking the real center of authority (frustrating clients), and eliminating opportunities to deal directly with the true decision-maker. Without well-designed procedures approval can compromise openness, comprehensibility, fairness, efficiency and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural safeguards required where executive approval is used
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an executive approval model is used, certain formal requirements should be observed: (1) give interested parties opportunity to address concerns not before the agency; (2) communicate an explanation for refusal to approve to the agency and include it in the record; (3) executive should give policy directions from time to time and Parliament should expressly authorize this practice in legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a decision is not approved for reasons outside the agency's record, the matter could be sent back to the agency for further representations. Requiring explanations and periodic policy directions helps clarify government policy and avoids unlawful fettering arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer exceptional, visibly political intervention over party-triggered appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive intervention of a blatantly political nature should be exceptional and visibly political rather than hidden behind adjudicative language; the exceptional model is preferred if political override is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model reduces routine use and places political responsibility clearly on the executive, preserving agency integrity when intervention occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: maintain Federal Court exclusive jurisdiction and error-in-law ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Court should retain exclusive jurisdiction to review federal agencies and one ground for review should be 'error in law', including lack, wrongful failure to exercise, and abuse of jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review can influence agency mandates by interpreting constituent Acts; courts play role in articulating legislative integrity and ensuring agencies stay within legislative scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative clauses should be abolished or replaced with clear deference standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Privative ('exclusionary') clauses are inappropriate: they are technical, obscure, can mislead the non-specialist, and do little to foster mutual respect between courts and agencies; they should be abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Parliament fears increased judicial review after repeal, it should expressly require in legislation that courts show reasonable deference to agency expertise — e.g., courts should not intervene on alleged errors of law unless the agency's interpretation is patently unreasonable. Parliamentary policy on judicial review should be expressed in plain language to avoid traps for non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency participation in judicial review should be permitted in an explanatory role
rubrics_metrics.description: Where judicial review puts in issue important questions concerning criteria underlying an agency decision, agency participation can help judges understand the agency's position; courts generally allow agencies to intervene in an explanatory role but not to address directly the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should confine interventions to explanation of their statutory interpretation and jurisdictional stance. Current law on agency standing in proceedings is viewed as overly restrictive and may merit reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability should be rendered directly to Parliament (Recommendation 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accountability that agencies owe to Parliament should, in the normal course, be rendered directly to Parliament through its committee structure, not through the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for institutional design: prefer parliamentary committee oversight mechanisms rather than delegating supervisory responsibility to Cabinet/executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, broad objectives in constituent and enabling Acts (Recommendation 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituent and enabling Acts should define an independent agency's broad objectives as clearly and in as plain and unambiguous language as possible, but should not normally attempt to spell out detailed implementation policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize administration's dynamic nature: detailed policy often needs to be structured within subordinate legislation, agency rule-making and decision-making processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary assent required to redefine agency role/duties (Recommendation 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary assent is essential where the goal is to redefine an agency's role and duties; parliamentary approval should be required through an affirmative resolution whenever the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act authority is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major substantive changes to agency mandate or duties should not be implemented solely through executive administrative acts; require affirmative parliamentary procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency dominance in subordinate legislative process (Recommendation 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the link between statutory decision-making and policy development and the importance of broad participation in setting policy, independent agencies should play a dominant role in any subordinate legislative process provided for by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency involvement in drafting subordinate regulation or policy is necessary to reflect expertise and to ensure policies guiding administrative decisions are well-informed and participatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal delegation of regulation-making authority to agencies and limits on executive approval (Recommendation 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an agency's mandate involves policy, it should be formally authorized to develop policy in the form of regulations; these regulations should not normally be subject to executive approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting regulation-making power helps agencies implement policy; where executive approval is to be used, the statutory scheme should make its scope and limits clear to avoid cloaking responsibility and confusing accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot exemption for agency regulations using notice-and-comment (Recommendation 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pilot project should exempt agency regulations that are submitted to a public notice-and-comment procedure from those requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act that precede registration and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This would streamline regulation-making for agencies that use public notice-and-comment, reducing duplication and delay prior to formal registration and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: accountability owed to Parliament, not Cabinet
rubrics_metrics.description: Accountability for decision-making is owed to Parliament; supervision exercised by Cabinet is delegated and Parliament should be cautious about delegating supervisory responsibility to the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain agency integrity, Parliament must distance agencies from the center of the political spectrum as much as necessary to preserve their independent role; choose institutional frameworks accordingly.
